paragraphs: Stochastic approximation updates a solution using noisy information, while constraints restrict which solutions are acceptable. This paper studies problems with linear constraints, including federated learning as a special case. Its LPSA algorithm performs the projection operation probabilistically: at iteration n, a specified probability determines whether the algorithm projects back toward feasibility.

The analysis examines a particular family of projection probabilities and step sizes. Rather than treating every update separately, the authors construct a continuous approximation involving both diffusion and jumps. They show that trajectories formed from appropriately rescaled final iterates converge weakly to solutions of particular stochastic differential equations. This is a statement about limiting distributions of trajectories, rather than exact agreement between individual runs.

Studying those equations reveals different long-run behaviors depending on how projection probability compares with step size. The central finding is an asymptotic tradeoff between bias and variance. This gives a principled way to reason about projection schedules: their frequency affects both computational effort and the character of the remaining error.
neurips-2022-asymptotic-behaviors-of-pro.tldr: LPSA uses probabilistic projections and a jump-diffusion analysis to explain how projection frequency and step size shape long-run error.

paragraphs: Random features approximate kernel calculations through randomized representations. This paper introduces chefs' random tables, a family of features for Gaussian and softmax kernels that does not rely on the trigonometric mappings used by standard random kitchen sink methods. Some variants produce positive features, an important requirement for the low-rank Transformer applications considered here.

One variant, optimal positive random features, combines positive and bounded features with unbiased estimation of the softmax kernel. Unbiasedness means the estimate is correct on average, while the reported tail behavior makes large estimation errors increasingly unlikely. The authors also show how readily computed statistics can reduce variance, and how orthogonal random features provide further variance reduction for this variant at every dimension.

The experiments span nonparametric classification and Transformers for text, speech, and images. The authors report new state-of-the-art results for low-rank text Transformers with linear space and time complexity. The contribution connects the statistical quality of a kernel approximation to its usefulness in efficient models: reducing estimation variability matters alongside reducing computational cost.
neurips-2022-chefs-random-tables-non-tri.tldr: Chefs' random tables provide non-trigonometric kernel approximations with positive-feature variants that reduce variance and support efficient Transformers.

paragraphs: Score-based representations describe probability distributions through local changes, an approach that works naturally when inputs vary continuously. Discrete inputs create a problem because ordinary gradients are undefined. This paper develops a corresponding representation for discrete data, called the Concrete score, so that modeling can still focus on how probability changes around an input.

The construction starts with a predefined neighborhood structure specifying which local changes are available. The score measures probability changes along those directions. The distance used to measure a change links the discrete and continuous cases: Euclidean distance recovers the continuous Stein score, while Manhattan distance gives the proposed discrete score. The neighborhood therefore forms part of the representation's setup.

The authors then introduce Concrete Score Matching to learn these scores from samples, including an efficient objective intended to handle high-dimensional inputs. Density-estimation experiments cover synthetic data, tabular data, and high-dimensional images, with favorable results against existing discrete-data methods. The work provides both a discrete analogue of the score and a practical learning framework built around it.
neurips-2022-concrete-score-matching-gen.tldr: Concrete Score Matching replaces unavailable discrete gradients with neighborhood-based probability changes and learns them efficiently from samples.

paragraphs: Data valuation asks how much each training example contributes to a model. Existing Shapley-based approaches often measure that contribution using accuracy across an entire development set. This can obscure whether an example helps or harms predictions for its own class, a distinction that matters when looking for noisy or incorrect labels.

CS-Shapley changes the value function to distinguish contributions within an example's class from contributions outside it. The motivation is that an example that damages its own class may deserve a lower value even when an aggregate accuracy measure does not clearly expose that damage. The theoretical analysis establishes that the proposed function is essentially unique under two specified desirable properties for classification data valuation.

Experiments evaluate data removal and noisy-label detection using four classifiers, supporting the method's effectiveness relative to existing approaches. The authors also examine whether values computed using one classifier remain useful for another. Their results suggest such transfer is possible for Shapley-based valuation, making the usefulness of an estimated value potentially broader than the particular model used to obtain it.
neurips-2022-cs-shapley-class-wise-shapl.tldr: CS-Shapley values training examples by separating their effects on their own class from their effects on other classes.

paragraphs: This paper studies online optimization when streaming data arrive at multiple computing agents connected by a communication network. Agents need to exchange information, but high-dimensional data or large networks can make those exchanges expensive. The proposed approach compresses communicated differences within gradient-descent-based distributed algorithms to reduce that burden.

The authors develop three versions for different feedback settings: full information, one-point bandit feedback, and two-point bandit feedback. Their regret bounds explicitly include the time horizon, compression ratio, decision dimension, number of agents, and network properties. Regret measures the accumulated disadvantage relative to a comparison decision, so its growth describes how well learning keeps pace over time.

For convex and strongly convex losses, the algorithms are proved to have no regret and match the time-horizon dependence of their uncompressed counterparts. That matching concerns how the bounds scale with time; the analysis still tracks other relevant factors. Numerical experiments support the theory and show reduced total transmitted bits, connecting communication savings with preserved long-run learning behavior.
neurips-2022-distributed-online-convex-o.tldr: Compressed communication reduces transmitted data while preserving the time-horizon regret rates of distributed online optimization algorithms.

paragraphs: Safe exploration is difficult when a reinforcement-learning agent encounters safety costs only occasionally and does not know them beforehand. The agent must learn while trying to respect constraints. This paper introduces an additional safety state that makes the available safety budget part of the information used during learning.

The safety state is nonnegative exactly when the constraint is satisfied. Its value also indicates distance toward a violation, and its starting value specifies the available budget. This representation lets the authors derive policies for scheduling that budget during training. Their approach, Simmer, therefore treats the management of safety allowance as an explicit part of the learning process.

The paper considers both constraints on average cost and constraints that must hold with probability one. Experiments suggest that adding Simmer to a safe-learning algorithm can improve training-time safety in both settings. For average-cost constraints, the authors also report more stable training and better performance. These findings support budget scheduling as a useful mechanism for safer learning, without establishing that exploratory violations disappear.
neurips-2022-enhancing-safe-exploration-.tldr: Simmer adds a safety-budget state and schedules that budget to improve safety during reinforcement-learning training.

paragraphs: This paper examines factual errors in open-ended language generation through evaluation, sampling, and training. The authors create FactualityPrompts and accompanying metrics, then study models ranging from 126 million to 530 billion parameters. In their evaluation, larger models produce more factual text. This differs from a previous finding about susceptibility to misconceptions, highlighting that the measured notion of factuality matters.

The authors identify generation-time randomness as another source of factual errors. Common sampling methods such as top-p can harm factuality by introducing randomness throughout generation. Their factual-nucleus method adjusts that randomness dynamically, aiming to improve factual accuracy while retaining generation quality. This makes the sampling procedure itself a target for improvement.

The training contribution addresses how models learn associations between entities in factual text. TopicPrefix supplies topic information to improve awareness of facts, while sentence completion provides the training objective. The authors report that this approach can substantially reduce factual errors. Together, the contributions show that factual generation depends on choices about evaluation, decoding, and learning, beyond model size alone.
neurips-2022-factuality-enhanced-languag.tldr: The paper measures factual generation and improves it through dynamically adjusted sampling and training that emphasizes factual associations.

paragraphs: FairReprogram addresses fairness when a trained model's parameters cannot be changed. Updating an entire large network can impose substantial computation, storage, and data costs, while model privacy can further restrict access. The paper instead learns a small addition to the input, called a fairness trigger, to influence the fixed model's predictions.

The trigger is optimized toward fairness criteria through a min-max formulation. Its proposed mechanism is to supply misleading demographic information that interferes with the model's use of the correct demographic information. An information-theoretic analysis explains why this can obscure demographic bias and identifies conditions under which the fairness goals can be achieved.

Experiments on language and vision datasets report better fairness improvements than retraining-based methods under two widely used fairness criteria, with substantially less dependence on data. These results support input reprogramming as a practical route to improving the measured fairness of fixed models. The theoretical conditions remain part of the claim: the paper does not present every possible trigger as sufficient for every fairness goal.
neurips-2022-fairness-reprogramming-ae77.tldr: FairReprogram improves measured fairness in fixed models by learning input triggers that interfere with demographic information used in predictions.

paragraphs: This paper studies sequential decision-making when candidate choices are graphs and their rewards are initially unknown. Molecule design motivates the setting: relabeling a graph's nodes should not change its reward. The authors incorporate this permutation invariance into a graph neural network model to address large search domains and graphs with many nodes.

Their theory assumes that the reward belongs to the reproducing kernel Hilbert space of a permutation-invariant additive kernel. They connect this kernel structure to the graph neural tangent kernel, derive a confidence bound for the network's reward estimates, and use that bound in a phased-elimination algorithm. The algorithm has sublinear regret, meaning its accumulated disadvantage grows more slowly than the number of decisions.

The regret guarantee depends on the kernel's maximum information gain, for which the authors also provide a bound. Notably, their guarantees do not depend on the number of nodes, even though reward uses all node features. Empirical results show competitive performance and good scaling, complementing the guarantees under the stated reward-function assumption.
neurips-2022-graph-neural-network-bandit.tldr: The paper builds graph neural network bandit algorithms with sublinear regret guarantees that are independent of node count under a stated kernel assumption.

paragraphs: Hyperbolic representations are useful for capturing hierarchical structure, but models using them can overfit when training data are scarce. This paper proposes generating additional features directly in hyperbolic space. The aim is to supply diverse features that still help distinguish the relevant categories, giving the model more useful variation during learning.

The method represents augmented features with a wrapped hyperbolic normal distribution. A neural ordinary differential equation module, supported by meta-learning, estimates that distribution. This estimation component addresses a central difficulty: a distribution inferred from very few examples can itself be biased, so simply sampling more features from it would not resolve the underlying shortage of information.

The authors also derive an upper bound on the augmentation loss that enables training with the effect of infinitely many augmentations. The role of the bound is to make that training objective usable without explicitly enumerating an infinite collection. Experiments on few-shot and continual learning report significant improvements for hyperbolic algorithms in scarce-data settings, supporting both the augmentation strategy and its distribution-estimation approach.
neurips-2022-hyperbolic-feature-augmenta.tldr: The method augments hyperbolic features using an estimated distribution and a loss bound that supports training with infinitely many augmentations.

paragraphs: HYPRO addresses prediction of event sequences far into the future. The paper identifies the autoregressive structure of existing models as a source of poor performance on this task. Its approach retains an autoregressive model but gives it a specific role within a larger probabilistic system: proposing candidate future predictions.

A second component, an energy function, learns to reweight those proposals so that more realistic predictions receive higher probability. This separates the task of generating candidates from the task of judging their plausibility. The hybrid model therefore supplements the base predictor with a learned correction to how probability is assigned across its proposed futures.

The authors develop efficient procedures for both training and inference, making the two-component construction usable for prediction. Across multiple real-world datasets, HYPRO significantly outperforms previous models on long-horizon event forecasting. Ablation studies examine the contribution of the individual components. The findings support combining autoregressive proposals with learned reweighting as an effective way to improve predictions over extended future sequences.
neurips-2022-hypro-a-hybridly-normalized.tldr: HYPRO improves long-horizon event prediction by using an energy function to reweight futures proposed by an autoregressive model.

paragraphs: A model's parameterization can affect the path followed during training, even when the underlying prediction problem is unchanged. This paper studies that effect through the connection between gradient-based training and mirror descent. Earlier results had shown that some overparameterized models follow trajectories that can be understood using a different optimization geometry.

The authors give a complete characterization under a condition they call commuting parameterization, which includes the earlier results in this setting. They prove that gradient flow under any such parameterization is equivalent to continuous mirror descent with a corresponding mirror map. This relates the choice of model coordinates to the geometry governing the optimization trajectory.

The correspondence also runs in reverse: continuous mirror descent with any mirror map can be represented as gradient flow under a related commuting parameterization. That direction uses Nash's embedding theorem. Together, the results provide a unified theoretical account of these connections. The equivalence concerns continuous-time dynamics and the stated parameterization framework, which define the scope of the characterization.
neurips-2022-implicit-bias-of-gradient-d.tldr: The paper characterizes a two-way equivalence between gradient flow with commuting parameterizations and continuous mirror descent.

paragraphs: Searching over structured objects such as molecules is difficult because the candidates are discrete and hard to enumerate. Autoencoders simplify the task by mapping objects into a continuous latent space where Bayesian optimization can operate. However, that space may still have many dimensions, leaving a difficult optimization problem even after the representation has been learned.

LOL-BO adapts trust regions to this setting, concentrating optimization within local portions of the latent space. The encoder serves two related purposes: it represents objects globally for the autoencoder and acts as a deep kernel for the local surrogate model. This design better aligns what counts as a nearby change in latent space with a local change in the structured input.

Across six real-world benchmarks, the authors report improvements reaching twentyfold over state-of-the-art latent-space Bayesian optimization methods. That maximum describes the reported results rather than a uniform gain on every benchmark. The broader finding is that search strategy deserves attention alongside representation quality: a useful latent space still needs an optimization method suited to its geometry and dimensionality.
neurips-2022-local-latent-space-bayesian.tldr: LOL-BO improves structured-object optimization by aligning local latent-space search with local changes in the original inputs.

paragraphs: In a linear contextual bandit, a learner chooses actions and uses observed rewards to improve future choices. This paper studies the case where an adversary can alter those rewards. The total magnitude of alterations over all rounds is denoted by C, allowing the analysis to express how learning performance depends on the amount of corruption.

The proposed algorithm follows optimism in the face of uncertainty: it uses uncertainty estimates when deciding which actions are promising. Its central estimation tool is weighted ridge regression. Each chosen action receives a weight determined by its confidence, subject to a threshold, making confidence part of how the learner incorporates its observations.

With appropriate hyperparameter choices, the regret nearly matches lower bounds both when C is known and when it is unknown. The remaining gap is logarithmic. The method also achieves near-optimal regret in the uncorrupted case, where C is zero. These guarantees address earlier tradeoffs involving computational inefficiency, restrictive corruption assumptions, or an excessive regret penalty from corruption.
neurips-2022-nearly-optimal-algorithms-f.tldr: Confidence-weighted regression enables nearly optimal linear contextual bandit regret with either known or unknown adversarial corruption.

paragraphs: Sparse mixture-of-experts models increase capacity by routing input tokens to selected experts. The routing decision depends on each token's hidden representation. This paper identifies a tension in that mechanism: learning to match tokens with experts encourages representations to cluster around expert centers, creating a tendency toward representation collapse.

The proposed method computes token-to-expert routing scores on a low-dimensional hypersphere, a space whose points lie on the surface of a sphere. This changes the geometry in which routing matches are assessed. The intervention directly targets the routing mechanism implicated in clustering, linking a change in score computation to the behavior of the learned representations.

The authors test the approach in cross-lingual language-model pretraining and downstream fine-tuning. They report consistent gains across seven multilingual benchmarks. Their analysis of both representations and routing finds reduced collapse and more consistent routing compared with baseline mixture-of-experts methods. The findings support the scoring geometry as a useful design choice, while the stated result is alleviation of collapse rather than its complete elimination.
neurips-2022-on-the-representation-colla.tldr: Computing expert-routing scores on a low-dimensional hypersphere alleviates representation collapse and improves multilingual benchmark performance.

paragraphs: Completing a partially observed 3D object requires knowledge of plausible geometry. Models that learn whole-object patterns can become tied to the categories seen during training. PatchComplete instead learns local geometric patterns at several resolutions, using the observation that different object categories often share substructures, such as the legs of chairs and tables.

The model learns these patch priors across all training categories. An attention mechanism associates a partial input shape with relevant learned patches, and a decoder turns those associations into a complete reconstruction. Sharing local structure across categories helps the model avoid fitting only the full shapes familiar from training and enables completion of previously unseen categories.

Evaluation covers synthetic ShapeNet objects and real ScanNet scans containing noise and clutter. The authors report improvements over the state of the art in novel-category completion of 19.3% in Chamfer distance on ShapeNet and 9.0% on ScanNet. These findings support reusable local geometry as a basis for generalization, including when observations come from imperfect real-world scans.
neurips-2022-patchcomplete-learning-mult.tldr: PatchComplete reconstructs unseen object categories by combining shared local 3D shape priors learned at multiple resolutions.

paragraphs: Vision Transformers can be expensive to deploy on devices with limited memory and computation. Quantization reduces the precision used to represent and process values, but low-bit versions can lose substantial accuracy. This paper investigates where that loss comes from and identifies distorted information in quantized self-attention maps as a central bottleneck.

Q-ViT addresses that distortion with an information rectification module and a distribution-guided distillation scheme. These components are designed to preserve the information needed by attention despite the reduced numerical precision. The resulting approach produces fully quantized Vision Transformers, connecting the compression method to the specific internal computation found to cause difficulty.

Experiments on DeiT and Swin backbones report substantially better performance than prior approaches. One example reaches about 80.9% ImageNet Top-1 accuracy and exceeds its full-precision counterpart by a reported 1.0%. The same example has a theoretical 6.14-fold acceleration for ViT-S; this is a theoretical speedup rather than a stated device measurement. The results show that carefully addressing attention distortion can make aggressive quantization compatible with strong accuracy.
neurips-2022-q-vit-accurate-and-fully-qu.tldr: Q-ViT targets distortion in quantized attention to produce accurate, fully quantized low-bit Vision Transformers.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to find a Nash equilibrium in a two-player zero-sum Markov game. Alternating gradient updates are a natural approach: one player moves to decrease the objective while the other moves to increase it. However, the objective lacks the convexity and concavity that would make the behavior of those updates straightforward to analyze.

The authors introduce entropy regularization into the game. This changes the optimization landscape in ways that make solutions more identifiable and the problem more efficiently solvable. Crucially, they prove that suitable choices of the regularization parameter allow gradient descent-ascent to converge to an equilibrium of the original game, rather than only addressing the modified objective.

The analysis gives a finite-time performance guarantee for the algorithm's last iterate, directly characterizing the current output after a given amount of optimization. This substantially improves the existing bound for gradient descent-ascent without regularization. Numerical simulations also illustrate faster convergence. The result makes regularization a tool for improving both the analysis and observed behavior of an otherwise difficult game-solving procedure.
neurips-2022-regularized-gradient-descen.tldr: Properly chosen entropy regularization improves gradient descent-ascent convergence guarantees for finding equilibria in zero-sum Markov games.

paragraphs: Dataset distillation compresses training information so a network can be retrained without retaining the full original dataset. This paper represents that information as compact, addressable memories. Its central observation is that classes can share a common representation, making it possible to store useful training content more efficiently than treating every class separately.

The method learns a collection of shared bases and flexible addressing functions that combine them into diverse training examples. Because the bases are reused across classes, compressed storage need not grow linearly with class count. The framework also supports queries beyond simply recalling the original classes, expanding how the stored information can be accessed.

The authors report state-of-the-art distillation results across five benchmarks, including accuracy improvements of up to 16.5% on CIFAR10 and 9.7% on CIFAR100. They also apply the framework to continual learning, reporting state-of-the-art results on four benchmarks and a 23.2% improvement on MANY. These findings support shared, recombinable memories as a useful representation for both compact retraining data and retaining information across learning stages.
neurips-2022-remember-the-past-distillin.tldr: Shared addressable memories compress datasets into reusable training information and improve reported distillation and continual-learning results.

paragraphs: Video-language models combine visual and textual information, but success on ordinary evaluation data does not establish how well they handle altered inputs. This paper studies robustness in text-to-video retrieval, where a textual query is used to find relevant video. It creates two large benchmark datasets, MSRVTT-P and YouCook2-P, to make such evaluation systematic.

The benchmarks include 90 visual perturbations and 35 text perturbations. Testing both sides of the retrieval task helps distinguish sensitivity to changes in video from sensitivity to changes in language. The study also compares pretrained models with models trained from scratch and examines the kinds of visual information the evaluated systems attend to.

Three initial findings emerge for the studied models: text changes are handled more robustly than video changes, pretraining is associated with greater robustness, and attention favors scenes and objects over motion and actions. These are observations about the evaluated systems. The benchmarks provide a basis for investigating those patterns and for assessing future progress in video-language robustness.
neurips-2022-robustness-analysis-of-vide.tldr: New perturbation benchmarks reveal that studied video-language models are more sensitive to video changes and emphasize scenes and objects over motion.

paragraphs: Spiking neural networks process information through binary firing events over time. Surrogate gradients help train these networks despite the nondifferentiable firing operation, but ordinary batch normalization does not provide the same benefit it offers in conventional neural networks. This paper attributes that difficulty to the additional temporal dimension and proposes a normalization method designed around it.

Temporal effective batch normalization rescales presynaptic inputs using different weights at each time step. The goal is to make distributions across time smoother and more uniform. The theoretical analysis interprets the method as smoothing the optimization landscape and indicates that it could stabilize gradient norms, providing a possible explanation for easier training.

Experiments on static and neuromorphic datasets report accuracy beyond the compared state of the art while using fewer time steps. The method also shows better robustness to hyperparameter choices than other normalization approaches. These results support treating time explicitly in normalization: the contribution is both a targeted adjustment to the training process and evidence that it improves accuracy and training robustness.
neurips-2022-temporal-effective-batch-no.tldr: Time-dependent input rescaling improves spiking-network normalization, with reported accuracy gains, fewer time steps, and greater hyperparameter robustness.

paragraphs: Few-shot benchmarks often assume that the classes in an unlabeled query set are known and exactly match those in the labeled support set. This paper relaxes that assumption: query examples come from an unknown subset of a much larger pool of possible classes. Some support-set supervision can therefore concern classes absent from the query set.

The authors show that this setting reduces the performance of existing methods and propose PADDLE to address it. Its minimum-description-length-style objective balances how well the model fits the data against model complexity, while respecting support-set supervision. Competition among candidate classes favors retaining those that best explain the current task's data.

The formulation is hyperparameter-free and can be placed on top of any base-class training. The authors provide a block coordinate descent optimizer with a convergence guarantee and linear complexity per iteration. Experiments on standard few-shot datasets and i-Nat show highly competitive performance, particularly as the number of possible classes grows. The contribution links a more demanding evaluation setting to an inference method that explicitly selects effective classes.
neurips-2022-towards-practical-few-shot-.tldr: PADDLE improves few-shot inference when query classes are an unknown subset of many candidates by balancing fit and model complexity.

paragraphs: Grokking describes a surprising training pattern: a model first overfits its training examples and only much later begins to generalize. This paper investigates that delay by connecting the formation of internal representations with broader patterns of learning behavior. It combines an effective theory of representation dynamics with phase diagrams showing outcomes across hyperparameter choices.

In a toy setting, the theory predicts how structured representations develop and how their dynamics depend on training-set size. The authors connect those representations to generalization. Their empirical analysis identifies four phases: comprehension, grokking, memorization, and confusion. Representation learning appears only in an intermediate region containing comprehension and grokking, between the other two phases.

Within this picture, grokking lies closer to memorization than comprehension does, helping explain its delayed transition to generalization. The authors compare the intermediate region to situations where resource limitations encourage more efficient solutions. The study offers a mechanistic interpretation within its analyzed setting and demonstrates how physics-inspired theories and phase diagrams can organize otherwise puzzling learning behavior.
neurips-2022-towards-understanding-grokk.tldr: The paper explains grokking through delayed structured-representation learning in a region between memorization and confusion.

paragraphs: Contrastive Intrinsic Control prepares a reinforcement-learning agent before a specific task reward is available. The aim is to learn varied behaviors during reward-free pretraining that can later support adaptation to rewarded tasks. The method connects latent skill vectors with state transitions, making the changes an agent produces central to its learned skills.

CIC uses contrastive learning to build behavior embeddings from transitions and skill vectors. It seeks high mutual information between them, so the skill representation and resulting behavior are informative about each other. It also rewards high entropy in the behavior embeddings, creating an internal incentive to explore a diverse range of behaviors during pretraining.

The evaluation uses the state-based Unsupervised RL Benchmark in its asymptotic setting: a long reward-free training period followed by a short adaptation phase with external rewards. CIC improves adaptation efficiency over prior exploration algorithms in that setting. The finding supports learning diverse transition-based skills as preparation for later tasks, with the stated evidence specifically tied to state-based inputs and extended pretraining.
neurips-2022-unsupervised-reinforcement-.tldr: CIC learns diverse skills through contrastive transition embeddings and improves downstream adaptation after long reward-free pretraining.

paragraphs: Feature attribution tries to explain a model's prediction by assigning importance to its inputs. Shapley values assess a feature's contribution in different contexts formed by other features. This paper questions the equal emphasis given to contributions across contexts of different sizes, since a feature may behave differently when little other information is available than when much is already known.

The authors analyze simple cases where Shapley attribution gives greater importance to less influential features. This establishes that its game-theoretic design principles can produce mathematically suboptimal rankings in some machine-learning settings. WeightedSHAP generalizes the calculation by learning from data which marginal-contribution contexts deserve more emphasis, rather than fixing their relative importance in advance.

On several real-world datasets, features selected as influential by WeightedSHAP better reproduce the model's predictions than those selected using ordinary Shapley values. The empirical result concerns how faithfully selected features capture predictive behavior. The approach therefore makes attribution more responsive to the information structure of the task, while the theoretical examples explain why adapting those weights can matter.
neurips-2022-weightedshap-analyzing-and-.tldr: WeightedSHAP learns how to weight feature-contribution contexts, producing feature selections that better reproduce model predictions in reported experiments.
